chunks.text: Morning. Morning. How is everybody? Good, thank you. Do you want to be there? You can have that seat.

Right. So, we had you in a year or two ago. Yeah. Slightly longer, I think. It was- Yeah. Yeah, a couple of years ago, I think. Yeah. Yep. Mm. And we're just, I guess, looking for an update on how it's going. Mm-hmm. So, I'll leave it in your capable hands.

Yeah. It, uh, it is- Oh, okay. Shut that down. That's perfect. So first off, thank you for the opportunity to come back and give you an update. For those that I haven't met, so I'm Suzy Keeling, head of science research at Beef and Lamb New Zealand, and I'll let Cara introduce herself. Yeah. Cara Brosnahan, principal scientist, animal health research at Beef and Lamb as well.

And so what we thought we would do today, rather than talk, I guess, and sort of, yeah, skim across the details of all the different components of the facial eczema program, is that we would talk to you about what has become affectionately known as the Sheep Poo study, which is the epidemiological study, where we have looked to get a better understanding of the prevalence and distribution of facial eczema across New Zealand.

So we'll spend a little bit of time on that, and certainly, if you're curious about other parts of the program, by all means, we'd love to hear the questions. For those of you that aren't familiar with facial eczema, so it's been in New Zealand for, I guess, documented well over 120 years now. There isn't a cure. Historically, it was thought of as a sorry, excuse me, North Island, predominantly, disease. But certainly based on recent years and evidence that we now have to date, it is spreading south, and Cara will talk more about where we've actually found evidence of facial

eczema. I guess the other thing to note is it is caused by a toxin known as sporidesmin, which is produced by a fungus that essentially lives on pasture. So that and the other, I guess, interesting aspect when we think about other diseases, is facial eczema isn't particularly-- it doesn't discriminate. So it does impact all ruminant species. And in the New Zealand context, it is certainly one of our most predominant endemic diseases.

But through the research that we have been doing, it is very obvious that it is in other parts of the world. So that has actually offered the program opportunities for international collaboration as well. So I'll probably hand over to Cara now. If we can have the next slide. Yeah, to talk us through. Yeah, go for it. Oh, good. So one of the first things that I wanted to cover is that we've had a significant discovery in the first part of the program, understanding more about the fungus itself.

So as you can see there, those are those little grenades that people look for down the microscope to know how many spores are there, and that determines the risk of winter and actual facial eczema management. So this was always thought of as one species of fungus. But actually, when we looked at the DNA, there are two species of fungus that look identical down the microscope.

One can produce the toxin that causes FE, and one actually doesn't have the mechanisms to be able to do that. So it's really important to know that these two are there, and that we can distinguish them, so that we can create better tools that are definitely for that toxin producing fungus. But also so that we can assess the risk better and more accurately for farmers. So we have a test that we've developed in the program as well, a PCR test, to distinguish these two.

And now we're in the stages of validating that for a commercial use, and part of that is actually understanding what the interpretation of that result means, 'cause it's all very well having a test. But if farmers and vets don't know how to interpret it, then yeah, it's kind of useless. So that's where we're at with that. So that's a very exciting discovery.

And next slide, please. And it was quite cool to actually name it toxicarius. Oh, yeah. That's- Yeah, that's- Sorry, I didn't- Yeah. So the long name for the toxin producing one is Pseudopithomyces toxicarius, and then the other one- Cara's really good at saying that quickly. And then the other one that's the non-toxic species is the Pseudopithomyces charterii, which is the previous name for what it was always called. So it is a little bit confusing, but given that it's toxicarius, we feel like it's a little bit easier for people to know which one's the toxin

producing one. And the other major piece of work in this program is getting farmers involved. So for the last three years, we've had an epidemiological study running to understand the distribution and prevalence of facial eczema in New Zealand. So not just where we assume it to be, but actually taking samples from across the country so that we know.

We've had really amazing participation throughout the three years. So in season one, just over 200 farmers, and then by season three, up to almost 300 farmers. So this is-- It's very hard to get people participating voluntarily, and the fact that it grew over time is, yeah, just a kind of reminder of how important this disease is for New Zealand farmers.

So next slide, please. So this is, yeah, the Sheep Poo study, because we did get farmers to send in sheep poo from a mob of sheep every two weeks from October to May for three years. So it was a huge effort. They did get results back, as soon as we got the results from the lab, so they were informed of their risk as well, but still a huge effort.

How many farmers, sorry? How many farmers? So in year one, there was just over 200. And year three, almost 300 farmers. So over the whole study, there were over 400 farmers participating. So I think there was about 150 farmers that stayed for the whole three years. Hmm. And then that changed in terms of the numbers and people for the rest of the time. So yeah Pretty impressive, yeah.

So if you can... Sorry, there are a couple of... Yeah, if you click one more. So the other thing is this is a massive data set that we now have that we can dig into for other purposes, and the largest data set on FE, I'm going to say in the world, because no one else is looking at it as intensely as us.

And yeah, over 30,000 records so far, and that's not including season three. So we think we'll get about up to 50,000 data points, which is massive. And the other thing about it is that it was longitudinal, so it's over those three years. And because FE is so variable year to year, it's really important to get that spread and not just focus on one year.

So it was that each farmer had the same mob of sheep they were following or? Each year they could do a different mob, but within the year it was the same mob, so that we could trace it around the farm and see what paddocks were at risk and what weren't. It also gave us a really big bank of samples to be able to test that toxic versus non-toxic strain. So we're working through those to understand where the different species are around New Zealand, if they are, in fact, different in different parts of the country.

So we'll get a lot more information there. And the other thing is fecal facial eczema spore counts aren't a routine diagnostic that farmers use, so it provides more information to be able to interpret results if they do want to use it, because it does give you a little bit different information than a pasture spore count because it's telling you what the animal is actually eating, so what the risk is to the animal rather than what the potential risk is.

So there's a little bit different there. Great. Next slide, please. So we did find that it's certainly not a North Island problem. So this is a snapshot of over the three years- We're in the red zone... where, yeah. What zone are people in?

So this is the highest spore count that was seen within that region over each year. This is red, babe. Over each year. Oh, there you go. Yeah. I'll talk you through. So green means there were no spores seen in that region, and then up to black, which is the very dangerous. So the maroony red is that moderate risk range, and then the yellow to orange is lower risk, but if you're continually eating those spores, there still is the risk of getting facial eczema.

But it's getting worse, what, just in totality it looks like? Well, it's just very variable between the seasons. So that- Just hot and wet, isn't it? Yeah. So you can see on the- Exactly... East Coast, obviously in '23, '24, it was hot and wet. Yes. Mm. And then it's traditionally the West Coast. Yeah. So it's a really important reminder that it's not going to be the same every season, which is why monitoring is so key.

And yeah, found spores down in Southland in the first year. We didn't see them in year two and three, but we did see them in Otago throughout the three years. West Coast, little bit of a caveat on that one. The first two years we could not get West Coast farmers to to join. So there was only a couple. Yeah. there, because they definitely do get facial eczema and clinical facial eczema. Not as many sheep on the coast either, is there? No. But it is wet, so. Yeah, exactly. That's a factor. And the dairy cattle there, they've definitely been having problems the last few years. Yeah. Like, is it- So it is, so the pasture- But what's the advantage of doing one or the other?

Does that have an influence at all?

Because if you don't graze so low. Yes. Yeah, definitely. So are you measuring that too? Are you measuring that too? Yes. So we've been asking farmers who are submitting samples how, like what their pasture height is. Yeah. Yes. So similar to internal parasites, they're all sitting in that bottom layer. So if you're not going down and grazing that hard, then you are reducing the risk. But often in summer you're short of grass too. Exactly. Yeah. So sometimes it's not an option. But knowing that that is a risk and then putting other management in places is important. Mm-hmm. Yeah. So this picture represents a combined, the good and the bad fungus. the toxin. Because part of, I guess, the complexity of this is we don't really know why it's advantageous for this fungus to produce the toxin in the environment. Like its end goal was never about harming animals. Mm. So why is it advantageous for this fungus that lives down in a particular part of the pasture?

Like is it so it can kill other microbes, so it can out-compete them? So all of that isn't quite clear. Mm-hmm. Yeah. You mentioned about you developing that PCR test. Mm-hmm. I don't imagine it's unique to New Zealand. Is it? The fungus? Yeah. No. Yeah, so that test not developed anywhere else?

No, because a lot of other places in the world are, it's not as bad as New Zealand. So New Zealand definitely has, I guess, the worst cases of facial eczema. Mm. But it is popping up more and more around the world. So Netherlands in 2019 had their first case reported of facial eczema. There's been a few reports in the literature in the last few years from Portugal.

Mm. Spain. Yeah. How do we compare with Australia? Yeah, so Australia, it's very confined to an area in Victoria and mainly in dairy. So yeah. Yeah. Not only understanding what their challenges are, but sharing our insights. Because if the longer term outcome is that we can minimize harm to animals globally because we can share what we learn here, then that is certainly highly beneficial. Mm. Exactly. Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Yeah. The liver was under such pressure, and it was fine under normal circumstance. Yeah. But then with the pressure of- Yes, the baby. Yeah ... lambing or anything, yep, definitely. subclinical FE might be is really important. So we've had, um- They don't transfer it to their lamb, do they? No. No. Yeah. It's just them. No. It's more, yeah, it's more that because they are so much under pressure through that lambing, then that's when it all comes out. And I think, yeah, the only other thing I wanted to mention about the SheepCo study, so all of the data, we're using that to build a predictive model for FE.

So it's using real data as well as 30 years of meteorological data and machine learning so that we're not biasing what we think the parameters might be that affect FE. We're letting the models run, and that will give a much clearer picture of what are those things that drive FE long term. So that's pretty exciting work.

The two years of the data and the Where the data is showing that it's looking really good, and then the intention is to test it on year three's data, and then have something available for beta testing for farmers this coming FE season. So there's lots of very exciting things coming out of it.

So I guess one of the things on reflection, as Cara mentioned at the beginning, we had high hopes about farmer participation, but we certainly didn't think that was going to be as successful as it was.

So that in itself, of setting the foundations for farmers to then start their own kind of management and monitoring going forward, and we've built that community. There's a WhatsApp group. There are farmers participating in webinars. So it's gone from being something that perhaps you didn't want to necessarily talk about openly, to starting to create that dialogue.

And it's also been the dialogue that we've started to build with the veterinary community as well. So one of the things that the program is doing is, has built a continuous professional development course for veterinarians, and so we've partnered with the New Zealand Veterinary Association for that. So that's going to be launched in the next six months, I think.

Yep. And probably the big thing that I think we've still got a challenge going forward is that awareness and myth-busting. So there, we spoke initially about the historic perspective that it's only a North Island problem. We've now got really solid evidence that it is a South Island problem.

So from the perspective of starting to have conversations with farmers in the South Island about what does preparedness look like, what does introducing FA-tolerant genetics look like? But also because they kept monitoring, they were able to stop zinc

Spotting hidden losses, so certainly to that educational piece and creating awareness about subclinical disease and what to look out for, the importance of that. And the big achievement for us, as I've already mentioned, is the trust and the partnership that we've been able to form with farmers.

It's just been so exciting to get the feedback, have the participation. It's a pretty substantial commitment, you're going out every fortnight, collecting information about your animals, measuring pasture, sending in the sheep poo samples, all of those. But having that real sense of ownership and participation in the program has just been so exciting.

I still get very passionate about it. And we can go to the final slide, or we can wrap up. So you've probably got the sense that Beef and Lamb is certainly not doing this alone. It is a genuine cross-sector collaboration, not only with our farmers, but also MPI as significant co-funders.
